p1: With the start-up transient removed by the warm-up, the sequential monitor and the quorum raise few false alarms. The quorum has FPR 0.0050 and the sequential monitor 0.0061, against 0.5052 for the NIS test with its χ^{2} threshold, whose false alarms remain frequent because of the miscalibration discussed in Section III-E. The fixed thresholds of the sequential monitor, the quorum, and the leaky accumulator rest on calibration moments inflated by the flat-start transient, so after convergence they are conservative. The sequential monitor detects 64.4% of the onset sequences within 30 cycles, the quorum 65.0%, and the leaky accumulator 51.2%, and their post-onset recall is 0.5256, 0.4285, and 0.4082. Detected sequences are found quickly: the median delay is 0 cycles for the sequential monitor and the quorum and 4 cycles for the leaky accumulator, with ARL_{1} of 1.64, 1.88, and 6.01. The misses concentrate in the Subtle tier of the additive FDIA and in the voltage-scale and drift classes (Fig. 13).
p2: At thresholds frozen on the benign calibration sequences, the continuous statistics run at realized test FPRs of 0.0124 to 0.0251, close to the nominal 0.01. Detection probability within the window is a weak discriminator here, because the additive FDIA and the branch outage above the Subtle tier are detected in at least 84.8% of cycles by every statistic, and because a statistic with more false alarms also alarms more often by chance after the onset. The post-onset recall separates them. It is 0.5892 for g_{k}, 0.5901 for Θ_{k}, 0.5518 for the sliding sum, 0.5402 for the EWMA, and 0.4681 for the single-cycle NIS. The difference lies in the two persistent low-amplitude classes. On voltage-scale cycles the recall is 0.4479 for g_{k} and 0.4179 for Θ_{k}, against 0.2600 for the EWMA, 0.2637 for the sliding sum, and 0.0750 for the single-cycle NIS, and on drift cycles it is 0.1967, 0.2046, 0.1475, 0.1925, and 0.0492. At the Severe tier, g_{k} retains 85.3% of voltage-scale and 50.8% of drift cycles, Θ_{k} 78.8% and 53.2%, the EWMA 42.2% and 34.5%, and the sliding sum 36.0% and 33.8%. At the Subtle tier no statistic exceeds 2.7% on these two classes. The advantage of the long-memory accumulators on the voltage-scale and drift cycles holds on the 9-, 14-, and 30-bus cases but not on the 118-bus case, where the recall on these cycles is 0.1158 for g_{k}, 0.0817 for Θ_{k}, 0.1608 for the EWMA, and 0.2300 for the sliding sum. On that case y_{k} exceeds κ=0.5 in only 2.7% of these cycles, so g_{k} rarely grows. With one class and one constant tier per sequence, the Moderate-tier dip disappears. For every anomaly class and every accumulating statistic, recall at the Moderate tier is at least as high as at the Subtle tier, and the highest recall falls at the Strong or Severe tier. This points to the interleaving of the original protocol, rather than the amplitude, as the cause of the dip in Fig. 10. At a calibrated rate of 0.05 the ordering is unchanged (post-onset recall 0.5906, 0.6109, 0.5573, 0.5484, and 0.4777).
p3: The two experiments agree that temporal accumulation of innovation evidence is more important than the single-cycle statistic or the voting rule. They differ on whether the accumulation rule matters. Under the reset protocol, every accumulator separates the persistent anomalies perfectly once the filter settles, and the CUSUM recursion cannot be told apart from an EWMA or a window sum. When the anomaly starts after convergence and thresholds are calibrated beforehand, the long-memory accumulators, the CUSUM recursion and the leaky accumulator, retain more of the low-amplitude voltage-scale and drift cycles than the EWMA with λ=0.2 and the 10-cycle window, whose memory is short, pooled over the four systems and on the 9-, 14-, and 30-bus cases, but not on the 118-bus case. The CUSUM recursion is not uniquely effective, since the leaky accumulator performs similarly, and these comparisons are empirical and specific to the synthetic scenarios, the single onset time, and the parameter values tested. Accumulation-based approaches to detecting injected data and drift have been explored in [13], [14]. The present results are consistent with their underlying motivation, although no direct comparison with those methods was conducted.
calsize: Over 50 to 400 calibration samples, τ_{comp} varies between 0.5552 and 0.8258 on the 9-bus case, 0.6503 and 0.8548 on the 14-bus case, 0.4140 and 0.6349 on the 30-bus case, and 0.7105 and 0.8622 on the 118-bus case. The ordering of the seeds changes with the sample size on the 9-, 14-, 30-, and 118-bus cases, so the 99th-percentile threshold is not stable at these sample sizes.
params: Table XVIII varies one parameter at a time on the original protocol. Over κ∈{0.25,0.5,1.0} and τ_{cusum}∈{3,5,7}, the F1 of the sequential monitor stays between 0.9327 and 0.9737, and the main effect is on false alarms: its FPR falls from 0.4592 at κ=0.25 to 0.1242 at κ=1.0, and from 0.3058 at τ_{cusum}=3 to 0.1942 at τ_{cusum}=7. The quorum stays between F1 0.9006 and 0.9234. The estimator covariances matter more for the NIS test and the quorum. Scaling Q by 0.1 or 10 gives sequential-monitor F1 0.9543 and 0.9360 and quorum FPR 0.2833 and 0.0383, against 0.9678 and 0.1525 at the reported setting. Scaling R by 0.5 or 2 gives sequential-monitor F1 0.9703 and 0.9645 and quorum FPR 0.1850 and 0.1333. The NIS test is the stream most affected by Q and R, with FPR 0.9958 and 0.0383 for the two Q scalings and 0.8542 and 0.2833 for the two R scalings, against 0.5358. In the onset experiment the same κ and τ_{cusum} grid moves the post-onset recall of the sequential monitor between 0.4533 and 0.5831 and its FPR between 0.0000 and 0.0441. The reported setting is therefore not the best on F1 within this grid, and the results depend on the covariance settings of the estimator, which were fixed a priori and not tuned.
concl: When the anomaly began after the estimator had converged and thresholds were calibrated on separate benign data, the long-memory accumulators retained the most low-amplitude cycles (post-onset recall 0.5892 for the CUSUM recursion and 0.5901 for the leaky accumulator, against 0.5402 for the EWMA, 0.5518 for the window sum, and 0.4681 for the single-cycle NIS), so under onset conditions the memory length of the accumulator also mattered, on the 9-, 14-, and 30-bus cases but not on the 118-bus case.
outage: A second outage construction checks the dependence on the fixed pre-outage state. It switches off the same branch, re-solves the AC power flow with PYPOWER, and generates the measurements from the physically settled post-outage state with the same tier-dependent state noise and the repository calibration, detectors, and measurement function (one 60-cycle sequence per case and seed). The largest change of a bus voltage magnitude between the pre- and post-outage solutions ranges from 0.00025 p.u. on the 30-bus case to 0.06789 p.u. on the 9-bus case. K=2 detects 0.9833 to 1.0000 of these cycles, against 0.9833 to 1.0000 for the fixed-state outage over five seeds, and the NIS test and the sequential monitor detect at least 0.9833. On these four branches the outage class is detected almost completely in both constructions, so its detectability here does not hinge on whether the equilibrium is recomputed.
